Chapter 9: The Gift of Memory and the Weight of Regret.
As the years slip by, have you noticed how memories can be both a comfort and, well, a bit of a challenge? In his later letters, the father finds himself turning inward, really thinking about how our memories shape who we are—and how some regrets seem to follow us, especially when we look back.
Imagine this: you’re flipping through old photos, or maybe a song comes on that brings you right back to a certain moment, or you walk past a place that once meant everything. Sometimes, those memories make you smile. Other times, they sting a little. And honestly, most of the time, it’s a mix of both. The father admits there are things he wishes he’d done differently—conversations he never had, chances he let slip by, moments lost because he was distracted or too impatient.
He tells the story of an old friend. They had a falling out, and neither found the courage to reach out. Years passed. When they finally reconnected, both felt the heavy weight of all that lost time. It really hit home that regret isn’t just about what actually happened—it’s about all the things that could have been.
The father gently encourages Su Yen to make peace with her own past, to forgive herself and others for mistakes and misunderstandings. He reminds her that almost everyone carries some regret, but the real trick is not letting those regrets control what comes next. There’s always time to reach out, to say “I’m sorry,” or to start fresh.
He also shares how important it is to cherish the good memories. He remembers those family dinners where everyone told stories, each person adding a new detail or a burst of laughter. Moments like that, he says, are the threads that keep a family together, even when time and distance try to pull them apart.
And as he wraps up, he urges Su Yen to keep making new memories, to really be present, and to notice the beauty tucked into everyday life. Sure, the future’s always a little uncertain. But the memories we create now? Those become the treasures we carry with us for years to come.
